work: Enarratio in Epistolam I B. Pauli ad Timotheum
source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. XIII (Montreuil)

1.title: Expositio capituli primi: Paulus apostolus Jesu Christi, etc.
1.title_en: Exposition of the first chapter: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ, etc.

paras.t: PAULUS apostolus Jesu Christi, secundum imperium, id est ab imperio voluntatis, Dei Salvatoris nostri, videlicet Dei Patris, qui est salvator per auctoritatem et principalem efficientiam, quoniam gratiam influit, et per Filium suum mundum redemit, et Christi Jesu spei nostræ, id est ab imperio Christi factus apostolus, qui Christus est objectum et causa spei nostræ. Voluntas autem Patris et Christi, atque imperium utriusque, unum sunt penitus, sicut et utriusque est una essentia, una potentia, indivisa actio foris transiens, loquendo de Christo in quantum est Deus. Patre autem et Filio ejus volente ac præcipiente, factus est Paulus apostolus: qui scribit Timotheo dilecto filio in fide christiana, quoniam hanc didicit et recepit Timotheus a Paulo dispositive seu instrumentaliter. Sicque Apostolus genuit eum quantum ad esse christianitatis, quod fundatur in fide. [Gratia, misericordia et pax a Deo Patre, et Christo Jesu Domino nostro.]
paras.en: [[1:1|Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ|Paulus apostolus Jesu Christi]], [[1:1|according to the commandment|secundum imperium]], that is, by the command of the will, [[1:1|of God our Saviour|Dei Salvatoris nostri]], namely of God the Father, who is Saviour by authority and as principal efficient cause, since He pours in grace, and through His Son redeemed the world, [[1:1|and Christ Jesus our hope|et Christi Jesu spei nostræ]]: that is, made an apostle by the command of Christ, which Christ is the object and cause of our hope. Now the will of the Father and of Christ, and the command of each, are wholly one, as also there is one essence of each, one power, one undivided action passing outward, speaking of Christ inasmuch as He is God. By the will and precept, then, of the Father and of His Son, Paul was made an apostle: who writes [[1:2|To Timothy, his beloved son in faith|Timotheo dilecto filio in fide]], the Christian faith, since Timothy learnt and received it from Paul dispositively or instrumentally [that is, Paul was the disposing instrument, God the principal cause]. And so the Apostle begot him as to his Christian being, which is founded on faith. [[1:2|Grace, mercy and peace, from God the Father and from Christ Jesus our Lord|Gratia, misericordia et pax a Deo Patre, et Christo Jesu Domino nostro]] [this lemma is printed within brackets in the edition].

paras.t: Et quia inter cetera episcopi officia est, falsam doctrinam exstirpare, seu falsis doctoribus obviare, ideo primo de hoc tractat Apostolus. Sicut rogavi te ex caritate et humilitate, cui præcipere potui apostolica auctoritate, ut remaneres Ephesi, id est in urbe Ephesina metropoli Asiæ minoris, quæ est pars Græciæ, quum irem in Macedoniam: cujus metropolis est Thessalonica, ad Græciam pertinens. Cur autem rogaverit eum, adjecit: ut denuntiares quibusdam, videlicet separatis ab ecclesiastica unitate hominibus, utputa pseudoapostolis et eorum auditoribus, ne aliter docerent, id est, ne aliquid nostræ prædicationi contrarium affirmarent, neque intenderent fabulis, id est fictis et frivolis narrationibus Judæorum, quæ nec sacræ Scripturæ veteris Testamenti nec rationi concordant, et genealogiis interminatis, id est infinitis quodammodo et inexplicabilibus generationibus, quas isti confingunt. De quibus in Talmud eorum plurima conscribuntur, quæ sunt inexplicanda mendacia, scilicet, quod Adam duas habuit conjuges, de quibus plures genuit filios. Ex quibus excæcati Judæi deducunt, conscribunt, et computant interminabiles pene progenies. Quæ fabulæ et genealogiæ, quæstiones litigiosas, vanas ac steriles præstant per occasionem, quia ad eas inducunt, magis quam ædificationem Dei, id est informationem divinam seu spiritualem, quæ ædificatio est in fide tanquam fundamento, et in his quæ fidem concernunt, ad recte intelligendum testimonia fidei, et bene exsequendum seu operandum præcepta fidei atque consilia.
paras.en: And since among the other offices of a bishop is to root out false doctrine, or to withstand false teachers, the Apostle treats of this first. [[1:3|As I desired thee|Sicut rogavi te]] out of charity and humility, though I could have commanded thee by apostolic authority, [[1:3|to remain at Ephesus|ut remaneres Ephesi]], that is, in the city of Ephesus, metropolis of Asia Minor, which is part of Greece, [[1:3|when I went into Macedonia|quum irem in Macedoniam]], whose metropolis is Thessalonica, belonging to Greece. Why he desired him, he adds: [[1:3|that thou mightest charge some|ut denuntiares quibusdam]], namely men separated from the unity of the Church, such as false apostles and their hearers, [[1:3|not to teach otherwise|ne aliter docerent]], that is, not to affirm anything contrary to our preaching, [[1:4|Not to give heed to fables|neque intenderent fabulis]], that is, to the feigned and frivolous tales of the Jews, which agree neither with the holy Scripture of the Old Testament nor with reason, [[1:4|and endless genealogies|et genealogiis interminatis]], that is, generations in a manner infinite and inexplicable, which these men invent. Of these very many things are written in their Talmud, which are lies past unravelling: for instance, that Adam had two wives, of whom he begot many sons. From these the blinded Jews derive, write down and reckon almost endless lines of descent. [[1:4|which furnish questions|Quæ … quæstiones … præstant]] [Denis: “which fables and genealogies furnish questions”], contentious, vain and barren, by occasion, since they lead into them, [[1:4|rather than the edification of God|magis quam ædificationem Dei]], that is, divine or spiritual instruction, [[1:4|which is in faith|quæ ædificatio est in fide]], this edification, as in its foundation, and in the things that concern faith: for rightly understanding the testimonies of faith, and for well carrying out or performing the precepts and counsels of faith.

paras.t: Finis autem, id est finalis perfectio seu consummatio ultimata, præcepti, id est legis divinæ veteris et novæ, imo et omnium præceptorum, est caritas, id est actus interior caritatis, qua Deus proximusque diligitur, procedens de corde puro, id est appetitu intellectivo seu voluntate a passionibus et vitiis expurgata, et conscientia bona, quantum ad intellectum, cujus actus est conscientia, quæ est applicatio scientiæ ad particulare agibile. Quum vero recte applicatur, vocatur conscientia bona. De tali itaque conscientia actualis dilectio oritur, quando videlicet intellectus applicat suam notitiam ad id quod vere amabile est. Et fide non ficta, id est sincera, non simulata. Procedit autem dilectio ex voluntate elicitive, ex actu intellectus ostensive sive directive. Intellectus namque voluntati ostendit quid amet, et cognitio via est ad dilectionem. Ex fide vero [procedit] sicut ex quadam fundamentali radice, actum dilectionis ad supernaturalem finem dirigente. Caritas itaque est finis præcepti, sicut et alio loco testatur Apostolus: Plenitudo legis est dilectio. Unde Salvator in mandatis caritatis legem atque Prophetas censet pendere. Tria quippe præcepta primæ tabulæ ordinantur ad dilectionem Dei. Septem vero præcepta tabulæ secundæ ordinantur ad dilectionem proximi, quam certum est ordinari ad dilectionem Dei, quæ finis et vertex est totius perfectionis. Sed non potest dilectio Dei esse perfecta et pura, nisi passionibus reformatis.
paras.en: [[1:5|Now the end|Finis autem]], that is, the final perfection or ultimate consummation, [[1:5|of the commandment|præcepti]], that is, of the divine law old and new, indeed of all precepts, [[1:5|is charity|est caritas]], that is, the inward act of charity by which God and neighbour are loved, proceeding [[1:5|from a pure heart|de corde puro]], that is, from the intellectual appetite or will purged of passions and vices, [[1:5|and a good conscience|et conscientia bona]], as regards the intellect, whose act is conscience, which is the application of knowledge to a particular thing to be done. When it is rightly applied, it is called a good conscience. From such a conscience, then, actual love arises, namely when the intellect applies its knowledge to what is truly lovable. [[1:5|and an unfeigned faith|Et fide non ficta]], that is, sincere, not pretended. Love proceeds from the will elicitively [that is, as the power that produces the act], from the act of the intellect by way of showing or directing. For the intellect shows the will what to love, and knowledge is the way to love. But from faith it proceeds as from a fundamental root, directing the act of love to a supernatural end. Charity, then, is the end of the commandment, as the Apostle also testifies elsewhere: [[Rom 13:10|Love therefore is the fulfilling of the law|Plenitudo legis est dilectio]]. Hence the Saviour judges that the law and the Prophets depend on the commandments of charity[[Matt 22:40||]]. For the three precepts of the first table are ordered to the love of God; the seven precepts of the second table to the love of neighbour, which certainly is ordered to the love of God, the end and summit of all perfection. But the love of God cannot be perfect and pure unless the passions are reformed.

paras.t: A quibus, videlicet a puro corde, conscientia bona, et fide non ficta, quidam hæretici aberrantes, conversi sunt in vaniloquium, id est ad vanas et falsas assertiones de observatione legalium tempore novæ legis, volentes esse legis doctores, eo quod sint in propriis oculis nimium sapientes; non intelligentes neque quæ loquuntur, id est propria verba. Quum enim asserunt cærimonialia legis nunc observanda, nequaquam intelligunt propriam vocem, quum cærimonialia ex sua natura fuerint figurativa: unde veritate patefacta, cessare debuerant. Neque de quibus affirmant testimonia Scripturarum veteris Testamenti, quibus suum propositum probare nituntur.
paras.en: [[1:6|From which things|A quibus]], namely from a pure heart, a good conscience and unfeigned faith, [[1:6|some, going astray|quidam hæretici aberrantes]], heretics, [[1:6|are turned aside unto vain babbling|conversi sunt in vaniloquium]], that is, to vain and false assertions about observing the legal ceremonies in the time of the new law, [[1:7|Desiring to be teachers of the law|volentes esse legis doctores]], because they are overmuch wise in their own eyes[[Is 5:21||]]; [[1:7|understanding neither the things they say|non intelligentes neque quæ loquuntur]], that is, their own words. For when they assert that the ceremonies of the law are now to be observed, they do not understand their own utterance, since the ceremonies were by their nature figurative, and so, the truth being revealed, they ought to have ceased. [[1:7|nor whereof they affirm|Neque de quibus affirmant]]: the testimonies of the Scriptures of the Old Testament by which they strive to prove their purpose.

paras.t: Scimus autem quia bona est lex Mosaica, non solum in se tanquam divinitus data, sed etiam per comparationem ad homines, si quis ea legitime, id est juste et vere, utatur, intelligendo et observando eam secundum intentionem legislatoris principalis, videlicet Dei, et instrumentalis, utputa angeli seu Moysis, id est, ut spiritualiter intelligatur, ad Christi mysteria ordinetur, et quantum ad præcepta moralia, semper servetur, quantum vero ad cærimonialia, pro tempore legis scriptæ custodienda fuisse noscatur.
paras.en: [[1:8|But we know that the law is good|Scimus autem quia bona est lex]], the law of Moses, not only in itself as given by God, but also in relation to men, [[1:8|if a man use it lawfully|si quis ea legitime]], that is, justly and truly, [[1:8|use it|utatur]], understanding and observing it according to the intention of the principal lawgiver, namely God, and of the instrumental one, such as an angel or Moses: that is, that it be understood spiritually, be ordered to the mysteries of Christ, and as to the moral precepts be always kept, but as to the ceremonial ones be known to have been binding for the time of the written law.

paras.t: Scientes hoc, quia justo, id est bonis hominibus, non est lex posita, id est imposita, divinitusque collata, sed injustis. Videtur huic contrarium quod ait Psalmista: Quis est homo qui timet Dominum? legem statuit ei in via quam elegit. Unde in persona justi loquens: Bonum (inquit) mihi lex oris tui super millia auri et argenti. Baruch quoque ait: Deus invenit omnem viam disciplinæ, dedit illam Jacob puero suo, et Israel dilecto sibi. Puer autem et dilectus Dei, est justus. Ad Josue etiam Dominus loquitur: Custodi omnem legem quam tibi præcepit Moyses. Josue autem justus fuit. Et respondendum, quod intentio legis est homines ad debitum finem dirigere. Ideo primus actus legis est, homines facere bonos seu regulare actus humanos. Quantum ad hoc, omnibus data et posita est lex divina, et alia quælibet recta. Denique lex datur per modum præcepti quo applicatur ad actus. Actus vero sunt triplices, scilicet: boni, mali, et indifferentes. Unde et triplex est actus legis, videlicet: præcipere, quoad actus bonos; prohibere, quoad actus malos; et permittere, quoad actus indifferentes. Sunt autem et alii actus legis, videlicet, cogere nolentes, punire prævaricantes, terrere seu pœnas minari. Quantum ad hos actus, non est justis lex posita, nec proprie quantum ad actum prohibitionis. Actus tamen qui vocatur præcipere, cadit super justos: qui subjecti sunt legi, non coacte, sed sponte: non terrore pœnæ, sed amore justitiæ; non subjectione servili, sed libera. Quantum ergo ad hos actus posteriores, non est posita lex justis, sed injustis. Et non subditis, id est perversis et Deo rebellibus.
paras.en: [[1:9|Knowing this: That the law is not made for the just man|Scientes hoc, quia justo]], that is, for good men, [[1:9|the law is not made|non est lex posita]], that is, imposed and conferred by God, [[1:9|but for the unjust|sed injustis]]. Contrary to this seems what the Psalmist says: [[Ps 24:12|Who is the man that feareth the Lord? He hath appointed him a law in the way he hath chosen|Quis est homo qui timet Dominum? legem statuit ei in via quam elegit]]. And speaking in the person of the just man: [[Ps 118:72|The law of thy mouth is good to me, above thousands of gold and silver|Bonum (inquit) mihi lex oris tui super millia auri et argenti]], he says. Baruch also says: [[Bar 3:37|He found out all the way of knowledge, and gave it to Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved|Deus invenit omnem viam disciplinæ, dedit illam Jacob puero suo, et Israel dilecto sibi]]. But the servant and beloved of God is the just man. And the Lord says to Josue: [[Jos 1:7|do all the law, which Moses my servant hath commanded thee|Custodi omnem legem quam tibi præcepit Moyses]]. And Josue was just. The answer is that the intention of the law is to direct men to their due end. Hence the first act of law is to make men good, or to regulate human acts; and in this respect the divine law, and every other right law, is given and set for all. Further, law is given by way of precept, by which it is applied to acts. Acts are threefold: good, bad and indifferent. Hence the act of law is threefold: to command, as to good acts; to forbid, as to bad; and to permit, as to indifferent. There are also other acts of law: to compel the unwilling, to punish transgressors, to frighten or threaten penalties. As to these acts the law is not set for the just, nor properly as to the act of prohibition. But the act called commanding does fall upon the just, who are subject to the law not by compulsion but willingly, not by fear of punishment but by love of justice, not by servile but by free subjection. As to these latter acts, therefore, the law is set not for the just but for the unjust. [[1:9|and disobedient|Et non subditis]], that is, the perverse and rebels against God.

paras.t: De quibus particulariter subditur: impiis, qui contra Deum peccant directe, et peccatoribus, qui peccant in proximum, sceleratis in se ipsos, et contaminatis, consentiendo vel cooperando alienis peccatis, parricidis et matricidis, id est parentum carnalium vel spiritualium interfectoribus, homicidis, fornicariis, id est, fornicationem naturalem committentibus, masculorum concubitoribus, quod est peccatum contra naturam, plagiariis, id est, qui alios lædunt, mendacibus, et perjuris; et si (pro quia) quid aliud vitium a prædictis, sanæ doctrinæ, id est veræ atque morali scientiæ, adversatur, huic lex posita est: prout Galatis dixit Apostolus. Lex propter transgressiones posita est. Quæ sana doctrina est tradita secundum Evangelium, id est in Evangelio; vel, Secundum Evangelium, quoniam consonat evangelicæ doctrinæ: Evangelium, dico, gloriæ, id est, quod annuntiat et promittit gloriam, beati Dei, quam Deus gloriosus in se habet, suisque electis communicat; quod Evangelium creditum, id est commissum seu datum, est mihi ut dispensatori, quatenus aliis ipsum annuntiem.
paras.en: Of these it is added in particular: [[1:9|for the ungodly|impiis]], who sin directly against God, [[1:9|and for sinners|et peccatoribus]], who sin against their neighbour, [[1:9|for the wicked|sceleratis]], against themselves, [[1:9|and defiled|et contaminatis]], by consenting to or cooperating in others' sins, [[1:9|for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers|parricidis et matricidis]], that is, slayers of their parents, carnal or spiritual, [[1:9|for manslayers|homicidis]], [[1:10|For fornicators|fornicariis]], that is, those committing natural fornication, [[1:10|for them who defile themselves with mankind|masculorum concubitoribus]], which is the sin against nature, [[1:10|for menstealers|plagiariis]], that is, those who injure others, [[1:10|for liars, for perjured persons|mendacibus, et perjuris]]; [[1:10|and whatever other thing|et si (pro quia) quid aliud]] (*si*, “if”, standing for *quia*) [the Latin reads literally “and if any other”], any vice besides those named, [[1:10|is contrary to sound doctrine|sanæ doctrinæ adversatur]], that is, to true and moral knowledge: for this the law is set, as the Apostle told the Galatians: [[Gal 3:19|It was set because of transgressions|propter transgressiones posita est]]. Which sound doctrine [[1:11|is according to the gospel|est tradita secundum Evangelium]], handed down, that is, in the Gospel; or, according to the Gospel, because it accords with the Gospel teaching: the Gospel, I say, [[1:11|of the glory|gloriæ]], that is, which announces and promises glory, [[1:11|of the blessed God|beati Dei]], which the glorious God has in Himself and communicates to His elect; [[1:11|which hath been committed to my trust|quod … creditum … est mihi]], which Gospel is entrusted or given to me as steward, that I may announce it to others.

paras.t: Gratias ago ei, videlicet Deo Patri, qui me confortavit in anima ad credendum, sperandum, amandum divina, et ad omnia bona agenda, ac mala toleranda, in Christo Jesu Domino nostro, id est per Christum mediatorem Dei ac hominum, per cujus gratiam et meritum confortatus sum; quia fidelem me existimavit, id est, prævidit seu existimando effecit, ponens in ministerio, id est in apostolatus officio ad docendum ac prædicandum. Qui prius, id est, antequam inter Jerusalem et Damascum Christum vidi et credidi, fui blasphemus, Christum negando, et persecutor primitivæ Ecclesiæ, et contumeliosus, id est injurias contumaciter inferens sanctis. Sed ideo misericordiam Dei, id est indulgentiam, gratiam et apostolatum, consecutus sum accidenter, non directe, quia ignorans feci in incredulitate, id est, ignoranter peccavi per infidelitatem, sicque peccatum meum excusabile fuit. Non tamen ignorantia hæc, causa fuit meritoria gratiæ mihi concessæ, sed quædam occasio. Superabundavit autem gratia Domini nostri Jesu Christi in me, cum fide et dilectione, id est, etiam fides atque dilectio, quæ est in Christo Jesu sicut in causa et objecto, mihi abundanter infusæ sunt: sicut et alibi dixi, Ubi abundavit iniquitas, superabundavit et gratia.
paras.en: [[1:12|I give him thanks|Gratias ago ei]], namely God the Father, [[1:12|who hath strengthened me|qui me confortavit]] in soul to believe, hope and love divine things, to do all good and bear all evil, [[1:12|even to Christ Jesus our Lord|in Christo Jesu Domino nostro]] [Denis reads “in Christ Jesus”], that is, through Christ the mediator of God and men[[1 Tim 2:5||]], by whose grace and merit I was strengthened; [[1:12|for that he hath counted me faithful|quia fidelem me existimavit]], that is, foresaw it, or by so accounting made me so, [[1:12|putting me in the ministry|ponens in ministerio]], that is, in the office of the apostolate, to teach and preach. [[1:13|Who before|Qui prius]], that is, before I saw and believed in Christ between Jerusalem and Damascus, [[1:13|was a blasphemer|fui blasphemus]], denying Christ, [[1:13|and a persecutor|et persecutor]] of the primitive Church, [[1:13|and contumelious|et contumeliosus]], that is, insolently inflicting injuries on the saints[[Acts 9:1||]][[Acts 7:59||]][[Acts 8:3||]]. [[1:13|But I obtained the mercy of God|Sed … misericordiam Dei … consecutus sum]] [Denis: “But therefore I obtained”], that is, pardon, grace and the apostolate, accidentally, not directly, [[1:13|because I did it ignorantly in unbelief|quia ignorans feci in incredulitate]], that is, I sinned ignorantly through unbelief, and so my sin was excusable. Yet this ignorance was not a meritorious cause of the grace granted me, but a certain occasion. [[1:14|Now the grace of our Lord hath abounded exceedingly|Superabundavit autem gratia Domini nostri]] of our Lord Jesus Christ in me, [[1:14|with faith and love|cum fide et dilectione]], that is, faith and love also, [[1:14|which is in Christ Jesus|quæ est in Christo Jesu]] as in cause and object, were abundantly infused into me: as I said elsewhere, [[Rom 5:20|where sin abounded, grace did more abound|Ubi abundavit iniquitas, superabundavit et gratia]].

paras.t: Consequenter ponit rationem cur gratia Dei abundavit in se, imo in omnibus iniquis conversis. Fidelis, id est verax fideliterque credendus, sermo, et omni acceptione dignus, id est maxime acceptabilis, gratus et amplectendus, qui sequitur: quia, id est quod, Christus Jesus venit per humanæ naturæ assumptionem in hunc mundum: juxta illud Baruch. Post hæc in terris visus est, et cum hominibus conversatus est. Verbum enim caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis. Peccatores salvos facere, id est ad salvandum et liberandum iniquos, juxta illud Joannis: Non misit Deus Filium suum ut judicet mundum, sed ut salvetur mundus per ipsum. Unde et ipse testatur: Venit Filius hominis quærere et salvum facere quod perierat; itemque. Non venit vocare justos, sed peccatores ad pœnitentiam. Quorum primus, id est præcipuus, ego sum, propter magnitudinem peccatorum meorum: non tamen simpliciter primus seu maximus, sed secundum aliquam considerationem, videlicet in quantum peccata mea certius scio et gravius pondero quam aliorum.
paras.en: Next he gives the reason why God's grace abounded in him, indeed in all the wicked who are converted. [[1:15|A faithful|Fidelis]], that is, true and to be faithfully believed, [[1:15|saying, and worthy of all acceptation|sermo, et omni acceptione dignus]], that is, supremely acceptable, welcome and to be embraced, the one that follows: [[1:15|that Christ Jesus came|quia, id est quod, Christus Jesus venit]] (*quia*, that is, *quod*, “that”), by assuming human nature, [[1:15|into the world|in hunc mundum]]: according to that of Baruch: [[Bar 3:38|Afterwards he was seen upon earth, and conversed with men|Post hæc in terris visus est, et cum hominibus conversatus est]]. [[John 1:14|And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us|Verbum enim caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis]]. [[1:15|to save sinners|Peccatores salvos facere]], that is, to save and deliver the wicked, according to that of John: [[John 3:17|For God sent not his Son into the world, to judge the world: but that the world may be saved by him|Non misit Deus Filium suum ut judicet mundum, sed ut salvetur mundus per ipsum]]. Hence He Himself testifies: [[Luke 19:10|For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost|Venit Filius hominis quærere et salvum facere quod perierat]]; and again: [[Matt 9:13|For I am not come to call the just, but sinners|Non venit vocare justos, sed peccatores]], to penance. [[1:15|of whom I am the chief|quorum primus ego sum]], that is, the foremost, because of the greatness of my sins: not, however, simply the first or greatest, but under a certain consideration, namely inasmuch as I know my own sins more surely and weigh them more heavily than those of others.

paras.t: Sed ideo misericordiam consecutus sum, ut in me, id est in mei piissima conversione et salvatione, primum, id est principaliter, ostenderet Christus Jesus omnem, id est perfectam, patientiam, id est longanimitatem et mansuetudinem suam, ad informationem eorum qui credituri sunt illi in vitam æternam, id est, ut omnes futuri fideles propter æternam vitam credituri, discant in me divinæ pietatis abyssum, quatenus nunquam desperent, considerantes me maximum peccatorem, in apostolum præelectum. Hæc est alia et major ac verior causa propter quam Deus misertus est Pauli, videlicet, ut poneret eum exemplum spei cunctis credentibus.
paras.en: [[1:16|But for this cause have I obtained mercy: that in me|Sed ideo misericordiam consecutus sum, ut in me]], that is, in my most loving conversion and salvation, [[1:16|first|primum]], that is, principally, [[1:16|Christ Jesus might shew forth all|ostenderet Christus Jesus omnem]], that is, perfect, [[1:16|patience|patientiam]], that is, His long-suffering and mildness, [[1:16|for the information of them that shall believe in him unto life everlasting|ad informationem eorum qui credituri sunt illi in vitam æternam]]: that is, so that all future faithful who are to believe for the sake of eternal life may learn in me the abyss of divine mercy, and so never despair, considering me, the greatest sinner, chosen beforehand to be an apostle. This is another, greater and truer cause why God had mercy on Paul: namely, to set him as an example of hope to all believers.

paras.t: Pro tantis igitur beneficiis gratias ago et dico: Regi autem sæculorum, id est Deo uni et trino, omnium generationum et temporum principi, omnia gubernanti, immortali, id est penitus invariabili, sicut et Jacobus loquitur: Apud quem non est transmutatio, nec vicissitudinis obumbratio; invisibili, quia nec oculo corporali, nec intellectuali perfecte et comprehensive videtur, id est omnino incomprehensibili, sicut apud Joannem habetur: Deum nemo vidit unquam. Quæ enim sunt Dei, nemo novit nisi Spiritus ejus. Soli Deo, id est Regi huic, qui solus est Deus, sit honor latriæ, id est summæ exhibitio reverentiæ, et gloria, id est beatitudo in se ipso; vel, Gloria, id est nominis sui clarificatio in cordibus hominum cum debita laude; in sæcula sæculorum, id est sine fine. Amen.
paras.en: For such great benefits, therefore, I give thanks and say: [[1:17|Now to the king of ages|Regi autem sæculorum]], that is, to God one and three, prince of all generations and times, governing all things, [[1:17|immortal|immortali]], that is, wholly unchangeable, as James also says: [[Jas 1:17|with whom there is no change nor shadow of alteration|Apud quem non est transmutatio, nec vicissitudinis obumbratio]]; [[1:17|invisible|invisibili]], because He is seen perfectly and comprehensively neither by the bodily eye nor by the intellectual, that is, wholly incomprehensible, as we have in John: [[John 1:18|No man hath seen God at any time|Deum nemo vidit unquam]]. [[1 Cor 2:11|the things also that are of God, no man knoweth, but the Spirit of God|Quæ enim sunt Dei, nemo novit nisi Spiritus ejus]]. [[1:17|the only God|Soli Deo]], that is, to this King who alone is God, be [[1:17|honour|honor]] of latria [that is, the worship due to God alone], that is, the showing of supreme reverence, [[1:17|and glory|et gloria]], that is, beatitude in Himself; or, glory, that is, the glorifying of His name in the hearts of men with due praise; [[1:17|for ever and ever|in sæcula sæculorum]], that is, without end. [[1:17|Amen|Amen]].

paras.t: Post divinorum beneficiorum recordationem, et humilitatis propriæ professionem ac devotissimam gratiarum actionem, docet Apostolus Timotheum quomodo in regimine gregis sui se habeat. Hoc præceptum quod subjungo, commendo tibi, fili Timothee, implendum secundum præcedentes in te prophetias, id est secundum revelationes propheticas mihi de te factas, antequam a me episcopus crearis: hoc est, sic impleas istud præceptum quemadmodum mihi Spiritus Sanctus revelavit de te priusquam te ordinarem episcopum. Præceptum autem est hoc: ut milites, id est, pugnando exerceas, in illis prophetiis adimplendis, bonam militiam, id est fructuosam exercitationem, resistendo falsis doctoribus, et veritatem prædicando, ac populum tuum regendo, sicut revelatum est mihi te operaturum, habens fidem plenam, et bonam conscientiam de nullo vitio sibi consciam.
paras.en: After recalling God's benefits, professing his own humility and giving most devout thanks, the Apostle teaches Timothy how to conduct himself in ruling his flock. [[1:18|This precept|Hoc præceptum]], which I add, [[1:18|I commend to thee, O son Timothy|commendo tibi, fili Timothee]], to be fulfilled [[1:18|according to the prophecies going before on thee|secundum præcedentes in te prophetias]], that is, according to the prophetic revelations made to me about thee before thou wast made bishop by me: that is, fulfil this precept as the Holy Ghost revealed to me concerning thee before I ordained thee bishop. And the precept is this: [[1:18|that thou war|ut milites]], that is, exercise by fighting, [[1:18|in them|in illis]], in fulfilling those prophecies, [[1:18|a good warfare|bonam militiam]], that is, a fruitful exercise, by resisting false teachers, preaching the truth and ruling thy people, as it was revealed to me thou wouldst do, [[1:19|Having faith|habens fidem]] full, [[1:19|and a good conscience|et bonam conscientiam]], conscious to itself of no vice.

paras.t: Quam conscientiam bonam quidam repellentes, id est peccando perdentes, circa fidem naufragaverunt, id est, in his quæ fidei sunt, erraverunt, et in profundum erroris submersi sunt. Ex quibus, id est de quorum numero, est Hymenæus et Alexander, quos tradidi Satanæ, id est excommunicavi, et excommunicatos exposui potestati diaboli, ut eos corporaliter vexet, donec resipiscant, ut discant per experientiam pœnarum suarum, non blasphemare: quemadmodum scriptum est, Sola vexatio dabit intellectum auditui. Sicque traditio ista finaliter intendebat in emendationem ipsorum. Tantæ demum potestatis, ut dictum est, erat Apostolus, ut recedentes a fide solo verbo daret diabolo: qui nil potest nisi a Deo et Sanctis permissus. Unde traditio hæc, fuit prolatio sententiæ ab ore Apostoli contra eos: qua dæmon percepta, mox traditos apprehendit, et tribulavit per intervalla; imo interim etiam occidit corrigi non volentes.
paras.en: [[1:19|which some rejecting|quam quidam repellentes]], which good conscience, that is, losing it by sinning, [[1:19|have made shipwreck concerning the faith|circa fidem naufragaverunt]], that is, have erred in matters of faith and are sunk in the depth of error. [[1:20|Of whom|Ex quibus]], that is, of whose number, [[1:20|is Hymeneus and Alexander, whom I have delivered up to Satan|est Hymenæus et Alexander, quos tradidi Satanæ]], that is, I excommunicated them, and exposed them, excommunicated, to the power of the devil[[1 Cor 5:5||]], that he might afflict them bodily until they come to their senses, [[1:20|that they may learn|ut discant]] by experience of their punishments, [[1:20|not to blaspheme|non blasphemare]]: as it is written, [[Is 28:19|vexation alone shall make you understand what you hear|Sola vexatio dabit intellectum auditui]]. And so this delivering up aimed finally at their amendment. So great, then, as has been said, was the Apostle's power, that by a word alone he could give over to the devil those who departed from the faith: the devil, who can do nothing unless permitted by God and the saints. Hence this delivering up was the pronouncing of sentence against them from the Apostle's mouth; which the demon perceiving, at once seized those delivered up and troubled them at intervals; indeed meanwhile he even slew those who would not be corrected.
